title: About Knife Recommendations
body: The first thing you need to learn about knife recommendations is to take them with a grain of salt. One person's criteria can be completely different to another's. Avoid a knife block full of knives or purchasing a set at big box stores — these generally have more knives than you need, cheaper materials, and worse fit and finish. A good setup: a larger knife (Chef/Gyuto), a mid-sized knife (Santoku, Bunka, Nakiri, large Petty), and a smaller Petty/utility knife covers 99% of needs. We are at an age of unprecedented worldwide access to kitchen knives. Websites from New Zealand to British Columbia sell their wares, but there are 10x as many opinions — which muddies the waters when hunting for the next knife. Try to triangulate subjective and objective information to determine what knife to get. Specifications give hard facts about a knife and can be critical in determining if a blade is right for you.

title: Everything is a Compromise
body: Choosing a kitchen knife almost always involves compromises. Key trade-offs: (1) Blade Shape and Profile: A chef's knife is versatile but may not excel at specialized tasks like filleting fish or slicing sushi. (2) Blade Material and Edge Retention: Softer stainless steel is easier to sharpen but may require more frequent maintenance, while harder high-carbon steel holds an edge longer but may chip if mishandled. (3) Handle Design and Comfort: Some prefer the traditional Wa handle; others find Western-style handles more ergonomic. (4) Price and Budget: Higher-priced knives often offer superior craftsmanship but balancing budget with quality requires compromise. (5) Maintenance and Care: Carbon steel blades need to be dried immediately after use to prevent rust; stainless steel blades are more forgiving.

title: Gyuto
body: The Gyuto is a Western design more commonly known as a Chef's Knife. The edge profile gives the blade more contact with the cutting board. Using the curve of the blade, relatively large portions of meat are easy to cut. This type of Japanese knife may not be the best choice for dense materials such as bone or cartilage, but is an efficient knife for medium to large vegetables or proteins. For a slightly shorter option with similar utility, the Santoku is a better choice. Ideal for: Chopping, slicing, disjointing some cuts, dicing, and julienning.

title: Santoku / Bunka / Ko-bunka
body: The Santoku knife originated in Japan. Santoku means 'three virtues' or 'three uses.' Traditionally used as a chef's knife by home cooks, it allows for various cutting methods with meat, fish, and vegetables. Also useful for slicing cheese, mincing meat, and chopping nuts. In the U.S., Bunka often refers to a Kengata Santoku — the angular triangle tip rather than the standard hoof tip. Many Bunkas have a flatter edge than traditional Santoku. Ideal for: Precision mincing, dicing, and slicing.

title: Petty
body: The Petty knife is a compact utility knife ideal for small and delicate work. Great for delicate cutting of small fruits, vegetables, herbs, and boning. Also one of the best types for cutting cheeses. Practically speaking, these are one of the first knives you would grab, even for simple things such as cutting up small pieces of chicken. Ideal for: Slicing and chopping.

title: Nakiri
body: The Nakiri style is designed for cutting greens. The blade is double-bevel, thin, and wide while the tip is flat and square. Mainly for carving vegetables — especially useful for shredding, chopping, or julienning. For the single-bevel variety, look at the Usuba. In Japanese cuisine, particularly useful for cutting vegetables such as daikon or carrot into julienne strips using the method called 'katsura-muki.' Ideal for: Chopping, slicing, dicing, and mincing.

title: Honesuki
body: Honesuki are a type of Japanese boning knife, perfect for deboning whole animals. Typically these knives have a thicker spine than most Western-style boning knives, allowing you to cut through cartilage. While not as thick as a Deba in the spine, the sharp drop tip can be used for fine slicing. Ideal for: Boning and removing skin.

title: Sujihiki
body: The Sujihiki blade is characterized by its narrow width and short height. These dimensions allow for less contact and friction across the surface area when slicing through meat, letting you slice through delicate fish in a single clean stroke — excellent for preparing sashimi. The blade has double-beveled edges. Ideal for: Slicing.

title: Funayuki
body: Funayuki is an all-purpose knife with a thin blade optimized for cutting fish. Mostly double-edged, blade lengths range from 12 to 21 cm. Funayuki means 'fisherman's row.' Initially used by fishers on boats to make fisherman's rice, a dish in which fish is processed, mixed with vegetables, and boiled. The design has a larger blade area and wider blade, making it easier to cut large vegetables too.

title: Bannou
body: Bannou means 'ten thousand abilities' — the idea being you get better than one knife in one package: an all-rounder that can manage every task so a full meal can be prepared from start to finish with just one knife. The difference between a bannou and a santoku? Nothing specific. Along with the bunka they are an all-purpose shortish general-utility knife ideal for home meal preparation. 'Bannou' is a catch-all name for an all-purpose knife rather than one recognizable style, so bannou knives by different makers may be very different knives.

title: Kiritsuke
body: This Japanese knife style is considered a status symbol among chefs in Japan, generally used only by a head chef due to the precise skill required. Its design is a hybrid of a gyuto and a yanagi. The edge comes with a single- or double-bevel, which broadens the functionality to include tap chopping. A better choice for an advanced home chef, though certainly a contender for a personal kitchen where you're the one in charge.

title: Yanagiba / Yanagi
body: Eastern Japan (Tokyo region) uses the name Yanagiba, meaning 'Willow Leaf.' To the west in Osaka and Kyoto, these knives are known as Shobu. The knife has a slim blade, somewhat similar to a Katana. Well known as a great sashimi knife, with a single-beveled edge good for cutting and fileting fish. Its pointed tip makes it possible to cut beautiful sashimi just by pulling in a single motion. Ideal for: Slicing.

title: Deba
body: Deba means 'a pointed carving knife.' Originated in Sakai, Osaka during the Edo period. Used for cleaning and cutting fish and birds. The blade has increased thickness along the spine, allowing it to cut off the heads of fish or through small bones without damage when used properly. The Deba should not be used to cut through thick bones. The Ajikiri is a smaller, thinner version designed for smaller fish such as mackerel. Ideal for: Slicing and disjointing.

title: Usuba
body: Used for vegetables, similar to the Nakiri. Originated in the Tokyo region and uses a single-bevel, thin blade. Perfect for peeling vegetables such as daikon due to the thin straight single edge. The straight edge makes it perfect for rhythmic chopping on a cutting board. Perfect for specialized cutting techniques like Katsuramuki ('rotary peeling') and Kazarigiri ('decorative cutting'). Ideal for: Chopping, slicing, dicing, and mincing.

title: Mukimono
body: This type of knife allows for stylized, intricate peeling of vegetables — specifically when designing peeled artwork to accompany the main dish. The blade is similar to an Usuba but the pointed tip allows for precision carving and peeling. Small, thin, and lightweight with a single-bevel edge. Ideal for: Slicing, dicing, mincing, and peeling.

title: Garasuki
body: Originated in Japan, where specialist chicken restaurants needed a knife to break down whole chickens. Like the Honesuki, particularly suitable for poultry and meat. The Garasuki shares the same overall blade profile as the Honesuki, but is larger, thicker, and heavier — a better choice when tackling larger sizes of poultry and cuts of meat. The 'reverse tanto tip' / 'clip point' design increases tip strength while still allowing it to easily pierce skin and make precise cuts in tight spaces such as joints.

title: Hankotsu
body: Hankotsu meaning 'Rebellious' is a boning knife that differs from the Honesuki because its shape is more straight-edged rather than triangular. It is used for cutting through hanging carcasses using a reverse cut grip. It has a pointed tip and a short height which allows the user to turn to cut along bone, connective tissue, or fat. Sometimes found unsharpened to give a very strong edge for tough deboning work. For poultry and fish, a Honesuki is generally a better option.

title: Kamagata
body: Originally designed to cut rubber soles for shoemaking, this rare shape complements any knife collection perfectly. Shallots, garlic, herbs, tiny diced onion and tomato, beef tartare — none can stand up to the small but mighty Kamagata. This uniquely shaped vegetable knife has a flat edge like a Nakiri, making it perfect for chopping herbs or slicing small vegetables like shallots or garlic. Its compact size also makes it great for line cooks.

title: Udon Kiri
body: As the name asserts, this Japanese knife type is dedicated to the creation of udon noodles, which require a unique shape in which the blade takes up less than half of the handle length. The Kiri also comes in soba and kasha variations, where the blade-to-handle ratio is slightly different, determined by the various noodle shapes. All three versions bear a long, straight blade with no curve, allowing for cutting straight to the board when pushing through dough while retaining a clean edge on every slice.

title: Cleaver (Japanese) & Kiri-cleaver
body: Japanese-style cleaver knives are ideal for slicing and disjointing. The heavy blade is useful for tasks like breaking down whole fish, meat, and poultry. Ideal for: Chopping, pounding, mincing, slicing, and dicing. A Kiri cleaver is a type of cleaver with a curved belly and a pointed nose, similar to a Chinese cleaver but with a different shape. More precise than a Chinese cleaver due to its pointed nose.

title: Chef's Knife (Western)
body: A multi-purpose kitchen tool that can be used to slice, dice, and chop ingredients with precision. Chef's knives typically have a sharp point and a prominent edge that features a sloping curve. The curve facilitates cutting and allows you to execute the knife's signature rocking motion. The shape and length of the blade can vary, but a chef's knife should feel like an extension of your body as it is being used.

title: Paring Knife
body: A paring knife is basically a mini chef's knife with a small blade offering greater versatility and precision. Great for peeling apples and potatoes, mincing small amounts of garlic and onions, and coring tomatoes. The blade is no longer than 3.5 inches, ideal for detail work like creating garnishes. Useful when working with small or tender vegetables and fruit — ginger, strawberries, garlic, and shallots — but not suited for harder vegetables such as carrots, beets, and squash.

title: Utility Knife
body: A kitchen utility knife is a medium-sized knife with a blade ranging from 4.5 to 6 inches. Used for tasks that would tax paring knives but are too delicate for chef's knives. Most utility knives look like elongated paring knives with a thin, pointed blade. Not to be confused with a pocket utility box cutter.

title: Bread Knife
body: Bread knives have a long, straight blade with a serrated edge perfect for sawing through soft items while keeping them intact. Some bread knives feature offset handles, designed to prevent the user's knuckles from hitting the cutting board. Blade length ranges from 5 to 14 inches, with 8 to 10 inches being most popular.

title: Carving / Slicing Knife
body: Carving/slicing knives have a long, narrow blade that tapers to a sharp point. Much thinner than chef knives, enabling them to carve thin, uniform slices from cooked poultry and large roasts. Many slicing knives feature granton edges, which reduces drag and prevents meat from tearing while cutting. Blade length ranges from 8 to 14 inches, with 10 inches being most popular.

title: Boning Knife
body: The blade of a boning knife is its defining feature: thin, semi-flexible, and with an ultra-sharp, tapered tip, explicitly designed for separating flesh from joints or bones with maximum precision and minimal waste. Its flexibility and long, slender shape makes it easier to maneuver between the spine of a chicken and the breast to separate meat from bone.

title: Filleting Knife
body: Very similar to boning knives but with a thinner and more flexible blade. The flexibility allows bending very far to cut close to the skin or bones. Can be used to cut fish. Due to the extra-narrow shape you can easily control the knife — so you never remove too much meat. Perfect knife when filleting soft types of meat and/or flat fish.

title: Steak Knife
body: Used for cutting foods served as a main course such as steak and chicken. Blade is usually 4 to 6 inches long and varies in thickness. Depending on the manufacturer, the blade may be serrated or straight-edged. Common in Europe to use a straight edge while most steak knives used in the U.S. are serrated. Since serrated knives cannot be sharpened, they require less sharpening maintenance, but eventually the serrated edge becomes dull and requires replacement.

title: Cleaver (Western)
body: Western cleavers easily break down meat, bones, and dense foods. They have a short, wide blade resembling an ax with a straight edge, useful for chopping and hacking with an up-and-down motion. Two types: meat cleavers (raw meat prep) and vegetable cleavers (thinner blade, better for vegetables and fish). Blade length ranges from 4 to 10 inches, with 7 inches being most popular.

title: Butcher Knife
body: Butcher knives have a long, curved blade with a sharp point at the end, helping with cutting through meat cleanly with a sawing motion. They feature a granton or straight edge to easily slice through meat without tearing or shredding. Blade length ranges from 5 to 12 inches, with 8 to 10 inches being most popular.

title: Cheese Knife
body: Cheese knives are smaller knives typically served with cheese for slicing and portioning. Several types with different blade styles and lengths, specially designed to cut through soft, semi-soft, and hard cheeses. Some are designed with holes that prevent cheeses from sticking to them for ease of use. Perfect tool for charcuterie and grazing boards.

title: Tourne Knife
body: The tourne knife, or bird's beak paring knife, has a short 2.25 to 3 inch blade that curves downward, mimicking the shape of a bird's beak. This allows you to closely grip the knife to peel small and odd-shaped food — such as a knob of ginger — with ease. The primary knife used to make tournee cuts: a French technique that involves turning and cutting vegetables into a seven-sided oblong, football shape to promote even cooking.

title: Breaking Knife
body: A type of butcher knife used for cutting large sections of meat into smaller, more accessible cuts. More narrow, thin, and curved than a traditional butcher knife, which gives additional leverage and flexibility when cutting through tough skin, cartilage, and small bones. Blade length ranges from 7 to 10 inches, with 8 inches being most popular.

title: Oyster Knife
body: An essential tool for any restaurant that shucks their own oysters. Several types are used for opening different sizes of oysters, but they all share a pointed tip that is perfect for unhinging the oyster's shell. Boston-style oyster knives are the most common and have long, narrow blades effective at opening oyster shells regardless of size — perfect for shucking beginners. Most feature an hourglass-shaped handle for a comfortable, secure grip.

title: Laser Knives
body: A 'laser' generally refers to an ultra-thin knife blade at the spine — blades that are 2.5mm or less in width on their spine, taper to a thin edge, and maintain this thinness throughout. Weight: approximately 6.5g/10mm or below is a good rule of thumb, so a 240mm Laser can be expected to weigh 156g or less. More likely to find lasers with harder steels (HRC 60 and above). They are light, nimble, and easy to sharpen, but more fragile because of their thin edges. As thinner knives have less steel in the blade, there is less material to introduce grinds that aid in cutting performance and food release. Sharpening removes metal — a thin knife has less material to lose over 10 years of sharpening. Laser gyutos are known for their incredibly thin blades (1.5mm to 2.5mm at the spine), lightweight construction, high-performance steel, minimalist blade geometry, and unparalleled precision cutting. Best suited for users who prioritize precision and finesse; may not be suitable for heavy-duty tasks like chopping through bones.

title: Midweight Knives
body: Midweight knives are the middle child — bigger than a laser, smaller than a workhorse, and the most common type. A common knife enthusiast trajectory for Westerners is to discover thin Japanese lasers, then discover the benefits of a properly ground thicker blade and want to try a workhorse. A midweight gyuto strikes a balance between durability and agility — moderate thickness and weight, providing enough heft for cutting through denser ingredients while still allowing for precise control. The blade typically has a versatile profile suitable for a wide range of kitchen tasks, with a moderate curve allowing for both rocking and slicing motions. They offer reliable edge retention and are comfortable to handle during prolonged use.

title: Workhorse / Heavyweight Knives
body: The term 'workhorse' captures knives that are heavier — generally with a thicker spine, often convexly ground, meant to be used a lot. Approximately 10g/1cm and above is a good rule of thumb starting weight. Workhorses are generally more robust and less fragile; the weight of the blade can do a lot of work for you; they feel solid and assuring in hand; and can make prep work an absolute joy. You generally will not find the nimbleness and balance in workhorses that you would in a midweight or laser. Best definition found: 'An undelicate knife that can use its weight combined with its geometry to process large amounts of products comfortably and competently.' If thicker, denser vegetables are something you prepare regularly (butternut squash, sweet potatoes), a convex heavier knife could be a great addition.

title: Knife Length & Height
body: Length is a personal preference reflecting your environment, your ingredients, and your preferences. Smaller kitchens may require shorter blades. If you cut a lot of large ingredients (e.g. butternut squash), you might need a longer blade. Height: Gyutos have been getting taller at the heel to accommodate more room for the hand. Western chef's knives have generally been taller at the heel. The agreed-upon new standard for the prototypical 240mm gyuto is 50mm in height. Things to consider: your height relative to the surface you work on (add cutting board height to that calculus), hand size, and how you cut (push/pull, rock chop, etc.).

title: Wa vs Yo Handles
body: With Japanese style knives you often see the blade with a piece of metal (the Tang) going into a handle. When the tang runs the full length and a handle is made by affixing materials on both sides, this is a Full Tanged, Western Style, or Yo handle. When the tang goes into the handle and you cannot see the end, this is called a Hidden Tang with a Wa Handle. After the fall of Japan in WWII, Japan began producing knives with full-tang western handles for export to match Western tastes. Fast forward to today, Japan's handmade knife market has been revitalized and Western tastes evolved to gravitate towards the more traditional-looking Wa handle. Wa handles let you customize your knife easier, move balance from the handle towards the blade, and are versatile for multiple hand positions. Wa handles are also easier to remove and replace without damage.

title: Why Western Handles on Japanese Knives
body: Several factors explain the prevalence of Western-style handles on Japanese knives: (1) Globalization — growing demand for knives familiar to Western users. (2) Ergonomics — Western-style handles with contoured shapes are often perceived as more comfortable, providing a secure grip and reducing hand fatigue. (3) Versatility — Yo handles are well-suited for a wide range of kitchen tasks and cutting techniques. (4) Availability — Western-style knives are more readily available in mass-market retail. (5) Stainless Preference — many Western-style knives feature stainless steel blades which resist corrosion and are easy to maintain. (6) Modernization — the evolving nature of Japanese cuisine has led to a blending of traditional and Western culinary techniques.

title: Wood Handles
body: Benefits: Aesthetics — Wood handles exude timeless elegance and add sophistication. Comfortable Grip — Natural, ergonomic grip that feels comfortable, reducing fatigue. Natural Insulation — Comfortable to hold in cold and hot conditions. Excellent Feedback — Wood's natural vibration-damping properties provide better feedback during cutting, enhancing precision and control. Drawbacks: Maintenance — Wood handles require regular maintenance (periodic oiling or waxing) to prevent drying and cracking. Hygiene — Wood is porous and can absorb moisture and food particles, potentially less hygienic. Susceptibility to Damage — More prone to scratches, dents, and moisture-related issues, requiring careful handling and storage.

title: Plastic Handles
body: Benefits: Durability — Highly durable, impact-resistant, and less prone to damage than other materials. Easy Maintenance — Generally non-porous, making them easy to clean and maintain. Less likely to absorb moisture or odours. Affordability — Often more cost-effective than other handle materials. Lightweight — Typically lightweight, providing ease of use and reducing hand fatigue. Drawbacks: Less Aesthetic Appeal — May lack the visual appeal and natural warmth of wood or metal. Limited Heat Resistance — Some plastic handles may have lower heat resistance, making them unsuitable for high-temperature applications. Potential Grip Concerns — Some may lack the same tactile feedback and ergonomic comfort as other materials.

title: Metal Handles
body: Benefits: Durability and Strength — Exceptionally durable, resistant to wear, can withstand heavy use without deformation or breakage. Hygienic and Easy to Clean — Non-porous, ensuring better hygiene and reducing the risk of bacterial growth. Sleek and Modern Look — Provides a contemporary and professional appearance. Heat Conductivity — Efficiently dissipates heat. Drawbacks: Weight — Metal handles tend to be heavier, affecting overall balance and user comfort during extended use. Potential Slipperiness — Some metal handles may be slippery when wet or greasy, requiring extra caution. Temperature Sensitivity — Metal handles can become extremely hot or cold when exposed to extreme temperatures.

title: Composite Handles
body: Composite handles are often made from a combination of materials like resin, fibre, or rubber. Benefits: Strength and Durability — Excellent strength with enhanced impact resistance and resistance to wear. Versatility in Design — Allow for innovative handle designs, providing ergonomic shapes and textures for improved grip and control. Enhanced Grip — Often feature textured surfaces or rubberized inserts, providing a secure and comfortable grip even in wet or greasy conditions. Moisture Resistance — Generally moisture-resistant, minimizing the risk of warping, cracking, or bacterial growth. Drawbacks: Cost — May have a higher price point than other handle materials. Potential Wear and Tear — Some handles may be susceptible to scratching or showing signs of wear over time.

title: Stainless Steel Overview
body: Stainless steel is generally any steel alloy with a minimum of 10.5% chromium content by mass. Compared to carbon steel, stainless steel Japanese knives are highly resistant to corrosion. The chromium oxide creates a protective film that prevents contact between water and iron or oxygen. Important note: stainless steel knives are not completely stain-proof or rust-proof. If exposed to water for a prolonged amount of time, they will rust, particularly if the liquid has salt in it. Hardness is determined using the Rockwell scale (HRC). Most mid-to-higher quality Japanese steels will have HRC 58 or higher, though chemical composition also impacts performance and should be taken into account.

title: VG-10
body: VG-10 is a great type of stainless steel for kitchen knives and very common. Typically these knives have an HRC between 60 and 61, good edge retention, and excellent corrosion resistance. Damascus-style knives often use VG-10 as the core. VG-10 is a grade of Japanese stainless steel primarily focused on cutlery. The name stands for V Gold 10, where 'gold' refers to quality. Approximate composition: 1% carbon, 1-3% vanadium, 14.5-15.5% chromium, 0.9-1.2% molybdenum, 1.3-1.5% cobalt, 0.5% manganese, and 0.03% phosphorus.

title: AUS-10
body: AUS-10 is a high-performance knife steel with sharp and rust-resistant properties. Offers slightly less chromium than VG-10 and may be more susceptible to corrosion but should have a little better edge retention to compensate. Composition: approximately 1.05% carbon, 14% chromium, 0.2% molybdenum, 0.2% vanadium, 0.5% manganese, 0.5% nickel, and 1% silicon. Hardness: 58-61 HRC. Molybdenum/vanadium is added to ordinary stainless steel, strengthening it more than basic stainless steel.

title: Ginsan / Silver No.3
body: Ginsan is a very fine-grained Japanese stainless steel that can have an edge sharpness and edge retention similar to some high-carbon steels. Generally thought to be slightly easier to sharpen than VG-10 while also slightly more susceptible to rust due to lower chromium content. When Japanese chefs choose stainless steel over high-carbon steel, they will often choose Ginsan. Ginsan-Ko steel was developed by Hitachi Metals and is composed of about 1.05% carbon, 13% chromium, and 0.8% manganese, with a hardness rating between 59 and 62 HRC.

title: ZA-18
body: ZA-18 was designed by Aichi to compete with or even outperform VG-10. Composition: 0.95-1.2% carbon, 17-18% chromium, 1-1.5% molybdenum, 0.1-0.25% vanadium, 0-1% manganese, 0-1% silicon. Hardness: 61-63 HRC. This stainless steel has very high hardness and can be sharpened to a razor-sharp edge. It is an incredible stainless steel with great edge retention.

title: SRS13
body: SRS13 steel, developed by Nachi-Fujikoshi, is an innovative powder metallurgy super stainless steel. Capable of reaching a hardness of HRC 64 through heat treatment. Artisans have the option to leave some flexibility in the heat treatment process, striking a balance between hardness and resilience — resulting in blades less prone to chipping compared to SG2/R2 steel. This makes SRS13 a preferred choice for demanding tasks, providing outstanding cutting performance without compromising durability.

title: SG2 / R2
body: Developed by Takefu Special Steel, Super Gold 2 (SG2) is a premium powdered tool steel alloy specifically engineered for high-quality blades. Heat-treatable to an impressive hardness of up to 64 HRC, SG2 blades exhibit outstanding edge retention and wear resistance. R2, produced by Kobelco Steel, is widely believed to be identical to SG2 in composition and properties. Due to their indistinguishable characteristics, these steels are often referred to interchangeably as SG2/R2. Blades made from SG2/R2 have gained considerable popularity among both professional chefs and knife enthusiasts for their exceptional cutting performance and long-lasting edge sharpness.

title: Molybdenum (Moly) Steels
body: Molybdenum stainless steels are a general class of Japanese steels that have a higher content of molybdenum than standard stainless steel knives. While all stainless steel knives have 10.5% or more chromium, not all have molybdenum. Molybdenum increases the corrosion resistance of stainless steel, making its use in kitchen knives particularly useful.

title: Inox
body: Inox is a general type of stainless steel, typically with a lower HRC than stainless steel types used in Japanese knives. The Inox used by Sakai Takayuki is typically AUS-8; often, this version of AUS-8 has molybdenum added to it for additional corrosion resistance. The HRC for this material is in the 58-59 range generally.

title: Swedish Steel / Bohler-Uddeholm
body: World-class Bohler-Uddeholm steel is considered the highest quality stainless steel material, with excellent sharpness, strength, and resistance to abrasion. Knives made of this type of steel are lightweight and easy to use. Bohler-Uddeholm is a large Austrian company that manufactures the steel used in the Grand Chef knife series. Established in 1670 in Sweden, they have a history of more than 300 years. The quality iron ore from their mines contains an extremely low amount of phosphorus and sulfur, so their steel has exceptional sharpness, excellent abrasion and corrosion resistance.

title: VS1 Semi-Stainless (VGin-1)
body: VS1 is a high-tech modern knife-making steel, prized for its ability to hold an edge and sharpen like high-carbon steel, with much less maintenance. Though this steel can rust, it doesn't do so easily and is relatively easy to care for. Also known as VGin-1 (Gin = Silver), Chromax Semi-Stainless Steel, or SKD12 Semi-Stainless Steel. Perfect for both home cooks looking for their first knife and professionals who put their knife through its paces. Composition: Carbon 0.95-1.05%, Chromium 4.5-5.5%, Molybdenum 0.8-1.2%, Vanadium 0.2%.

title: ZDP-189 Powdered Stainless
body: ZDP-189 was developed by Hitachi Metals Ltd. and is a true next-generation powdered steel. It can be hardened to a dizzying 65-67 Rockwell, giving you an extremely long-lived edge. With that extreme hardness comes a knife that is also extremely hard to sharpen; for home sharpeners this steel may feel like Everest to get an edge on. ZDP-189 is not widely used by blacksmiths and knifemakers due to the special forging and heat-treatment requirements. This steel can also be found under the name MC66 when used by Zwilling. ZDP-189 contains 3% Carbon and 20% Chromium; the remaining make-up is proprietary.

title: SLD Semi-Stainless
body: SLD semi-stainless steel was originally designed by Hitachi for cutting other steels. It holds an edge as long as carbon steel but is much easier to care for. SLD isn't completely stainless, so clean and dry it when you're done using it. Composition: Carbon 1.5%, Silicon 0.3%, Manganese 0.4%, Chromium 12%, Molybdenum 0.9%, Vanadium 0.3%.

title: SKD / SKD-12
body: SKD is the Japanese version of A2. It has finer carbides than SLD, but still provides a nice, toothy edge. Tougher due to the carbide volume difference. Not a real stainless — it will stain and rust if not cared for. Considered by many enthusiasts as one of the best semi-stainless steels available.

title: HAP40 High Speed Powder Semi-Stainless
body: Hitachi's HAP40 strikes a balance between hardness, toughness, and wear resistance to provide some of the best edge retention available. It can rust and will definitely stain, but is more forgiving than white or blue carbon steels. Make sure to wash and dry directly after use. After a nice strong patina has formed on the blade they are less likely to rust — patina is your friend! Composition: Carbon 1.27-1.33%, Chromium 3.7-4.7%, Molybdenum 4.6-5.4%, Tungsten 5.6-6.4%, Vanadium 2.8-3.3%, Cobalt 7.5-8.5%.

title: High Speed Powder Stainless Group (R2, SG2, SRS13, SRS15)
body: This group includes SRS13, SRS15, R2, and SG2 Powdered Stainless Steels. They all have a Rockwell hardness of 62-63 and are all very similar steels. These are serious precision instruments and must be treated as such — they need to be babied a bit because of the high hardness, especially when ground very thin. With these knives, one must accept that the blade could chip from time to time, but it's a small price to pay for the insane performance. Composition: Carbon 1.25-1.5%, Chromium 13-16%, Molybdenum 2.3-3.3%, Vanadium 1.5-2.2%, Manganese 0.3-0.4%, Silicon 0.3-0.5%. ZDP189 would also be considered a High-Speed Powder Stainless Steel but is significantly harder.

title: Cobalt Special Steel
body: Produced by the Takefu Special Steel Company, Cobalt Special Steel is formulated to offer incomparable corrosion resistance due to its 1.1% carbon and 16% chromium content. Tungsten is added to provide greater temper resistance, molybdenum offers superior rust resistance, and vanadium creates a finer microstructure. The addition of cobalt increases strength while giving a long-lasting, sharp edge. Category: Powdered Stainless Steel. HRC: 60-62.

title: ATS-34
body: ATS-34 Steel is Hitachi Steel's version of 154CM — an ingot alloy targeting the middle to higher-end knife segment. With 14% chromium it is quite corrosion resistant. The steel can be treated to a hardness of 60-61, offering adequate edge retention, but shows more toughness properties and is therefore better suited for heavier duty kitchen work. Also referred to as the Japanese equivalent of 154CM.

title: VG5
body: VG5 is a stainless steel used in some Japanese kitchen knives. Composition: Carbon 0.70-0.80%, Chromium 13-15%, Molybdenum 0.2-0.4%, Vanadium 0.10-0.20%.

title: Hagane / Yasugi Steel Overview
body: Hagane steel is the traditional method of melting iron sand in a clay furnace and adding carbon by mixing it with charcoal. Yasugi steel (or Yasugi hagane), produced by Hitachi Metals Ltd in Shimane prefecture, is the modern version of traditional Hagane. There are three main top-grade high-carbon Japanese steels: Shirogami or White Steel (#1, #2), Aogami or Blue Steel (#1, #2), and Aogami Super or Blue Super Steel. Yasugi steel is high-grade cutting steel with high purity. A high level of craftsmanship is required — generally only master craftsmen handle this type of metal when forging knives. While Yasugi steel allows for a razor-sharp edge (often used to make swords in ancient times), it is more prone to rusting and requires more care and maintenance.

title: Shirogami #1 / White Steel #1
body: Shirogami #1 has higher carbon content than Shirogami #2. The higher the carbon content, the better a knife holds an edge — however, it also becomes more brittle. This is a rigid material containing pure fine-grained carbon with very few contaminates within the iron. Used in the manufacture of the Honyaki knife via the traditional smithing process. There are only a few knife craftsmen who can bring out the real value of this material, even in Sakai. These knives can be sharpened to a razor's edge. Composition: approximately 1.2-1.4% carbon, 0.25% manganese. Hardness: 61-64 HRC.

title: Shirogami #2 / White Steel #2
body: Shirogami #2 is one of the most common types of high-carbon knife steels for handcrafted traditional Japanese kitchen knives. The composition is virtually the same as Shirogami #1 but with slightly lower carbon content (1.0-1.2% carbon). This allows the knife to be less prone to chipping and is generally preferred by most chefs. It is also easier to sharpen than Shirogami #1. Many sushi chefs will choose Shirogami #2 as it is less brittle and less likely to chip. Composition: 1.0-1.2% carbon, 0.25% manganese. Hardness: 60-63 HRC.

title: Aogami #1 / Blue Steel #1
body: Aogami #1 has the same carbon content as White Steel #1 — the difference is the addition of tungsten and chromium. These additions add specific qualities to already high-quality steel. Composition: about 1.3% carbon and 0.4% chromium added to the basic white steel, plus tungsten. Hardness: 61-64 HRC. High-grade Japanese steel that strengthens heat treatment characteristics and wear resistance. The sharpness lasts longer and cuts smoothly, so the cut is finished clean.

title: Aogami #2 / Blue Steel #2
body: Aogami #2 is one of the most common high-carbon steels found in Western-style, double-bevel Japanese kitchen knives. Similar to Shirogami #2 with 1.0-1.2% carbon, but tungsten and chromium are added to increase durability and abrasion resistance. Generally speaking, the differences between Aogami (Blue Steel) and Shirogami (White Steel) are that it is harder to break and the sharpness lasts longer. Shirogami is easier to sharpen than Aogami due to the addition of tungsten.

title: Aogami Super / Blue Super Steel
body: Aogami Super is composed of all the chemical components of Blue Steel #1, but with the addition of molybdenum and vanadium. These help increase corrosion resistance and strength respectively. Hardness: 61-65 HRC. Considered the best Yasugi steel, with excellent hardness and abrasion resistance. Note that Aogami Super is also harder to sharpen due to the addition of tungsten and vanadium. It is a favourite among blacksmiths and knife enthusiasts for its exceptional performance.

title: SK4 Carbon Steel
body: SK4 is a Japanese carbon steel used in some kitchen knives. Composition: Carbon 0.9-1.0%, Chromium 0.3%, Manganese 0.1-0.5%, Nickel 0.25%, Silicon 0.1-0.35%, Copper 0.25%.

title: Takefu V1 & V2
body: V-Toku2 is an excellent alloy steel within the Takefu 'V-Steel' range. Advantages: Low impurity, Easy Heat Treatment, Strong Temper, Good Processing (Hot Forging). The elements Chromium, Tungsten, and Vanadium form hard and compact carbide in the steel which improves durability. High hardness and high strength are achieved by the addition of Tungsten, which combined with Chromium enhances the steel properties, producing a well-balanced steel that makes annealing easier and improves hardenability.

title: AEB-L
body: AEB-L is a very common steel from Europe originally developed by Bohler-Uddeholm as a razor blade steel — it takes a very keen edge. The steel is chemically similar to the Sandvik series of steels (12C27 and 14C28N) and is almost identical to Sandvik's 13C27 with only minor differences in chemical composition. AEB-L enjoys a very good reputation among makers as a very consistent steel. It has a very basic heat treat, similar to 440C. It can be worked with relative ease on a grinder and can easily take a full mirror polish.

title: CPM MagnaCut
body: MagnaCut was introduced in 2021 and is the brainchild of knife steel guru Larrin Thomas, who designed the steel specifically for knives. Produced by Crucible, it's a powder metallurgy steel that exhibits very interesting and fairly unique properties. It provides an excellent mix of toughness and wear resistance while also maintaining high levels of corrosion resistance. The key is eliminating chromium carbides and maximizing free chromium through an optimal chromium-carbon balance. MagnaCut puts it in the same league as CPM-CruWear and CPM-4V for toughness and edge retention while eclipsing CPM-S45VN and CPM-S110V in corrosion resistance. A very interesting steel that will probably only get more popular. (Reference: knifesteelnerds.com)

title: Apex Ultra
body: ApexUltra is a steel specially developed for handmade knives. With its high purity and well-balanced alloy composition, it has the highest toughness of all knife steels tested so far in the 66+ HRC range, along with excellent edge retention. With its combination of high hardness and toughness, ApexUltra works very well with thin and sharp edges — kitchen knives, razors, and carving knives are examples of good applications. The forging and welding behaviour is described as similar to 52100. Most steels contain inclusions that do not benefit the steel and represent small defects. ApexUltra is designed with high purity and homogeneity, so the overall blade is durable throughout with no soft or brittle spots.

title: X50CrMoV15
body: X50CrMoV15 is the most used type of stainless steel for kitchen knives by German manufacturers and is a good type of steel for a very large audience. The corrosion resistance is very good and the cutting qualities are great. Great for family use and professional use where not everyone handles the knives with the same care. FYI: X stands for stainless, 50 for 0.50% carbon, and 15 for 15% chromium. The steel also contains small amounts of Molybdenum and Vanadium to improve the grain structure and wear resistance.

title: Cromova 18
body: Cromova is the name Global uses for the stainless steel they use. The steel is comprised of 0.8% carbon and the addition of chromium, molybdenum, and vanadium. Cromova steel has a fine grain structure and can be sharpened razor-sharp. It combines good cutting qualities with corrosion resistance.

title: Friodur
body: Friodur steel is a stainless type of steel mostly used by J.A. Henckels / Zwilling kitchen knives. The remarkable aspect is the heat treatment: first the steel is heated up, then the whole is cooled down to -70 degrees Celsius. This makes the knife even harder and more corrosion resistant.

title: 440A and 440C
body: 440 steel is a stainless type of steel that retains its sharpness well and is also corrosion resistant. For 440A steel the emphasis is placed on corrosion resistance. While 440C focuses on hardness — with the right heat treatment it can become the hardest and most wear-resistant type of steel ever produced. The key difference is carbon percentage. 440A: 0.60-0.75% carbon. 440C: 0.95-1.2% carbon (higher carbon = better edge retention, slightly less corrosion resistance).

title: Sandvik 12C27 and 14C28N
body: Sandvik is a producer of different stainless types of steel. The most famous type is 12C27, used for popular Morakniv knives as well as Opinel and Laguiole. This type of steel is easy to modify, retains its sharpness well, and is easy to sharpen. Sandvik 14C28N steel can be compared to 12C27 but contains additional nitrogen and slightly more carbon — making the knife a little more tough and wear resistant. Both are excellent value-for-money steels.

title: N680
body: N680 steel contains about 0.20% nitrogen and over 17% chromium, making it extremely corrosion resistant. If your blade will be in frequent contact with salt water, this is the steel for you. It is also a fine-grained steel that can take a very fine edge. Edge Retention: 5/10. Corrosion Resistance: 8/10. Ease of Sharpening: 6/10. Consider it a cheaper alternative to H1 steel with decent edge retention, though it won't hold an edge as long as 154CM.

title: 154CM
body: 154CM is a relatively hard steel considered an upgraded version of 440C through the addition of Molybdenum. This achieves superior edge holding compared to 440C while retaining similar excellent corrosion resistance. It has decent toughness good enough for most uses and holds an edge well. Edge Retention: 6/10. Corrosion Resistance: 6/10. Ease of Sharpening: 5/10. Also available as CPM 154 (a powder version of the same alloy), which is slightly superior in toughness and edge retention. Sweden's Damasteel also produces a similar grade in RWL-34.

title: On Cheaper Western Steels (Editorial)
body: Compelling arguments can be made for using 'cheaper' steel. Few reputable makers knowingly waste time and energy making knives out of compromised or inferior materials. Of Western steels, AEB-L, Sandvik, and 52100 (maybe CPM-154 and CPM D2) are fantastic for kitchen knives. Great heat treats of these steels produce knives that can take VERY keen edges, are tough, and keep edges a respectable time. The new super steels beat the cheaper steels in about every respect, but they are much harder to work with and the material is more expensive. Especially with the home chef, those improved attributes aren't going to contribute as much as they cost you. At a certain point you have a decreased return-on-investment. You don't have to break the bank to get stellar performance out of a kitchen knife.

1.4116 is a stainless type of steel with a high carbon content, used among others for the famous Swiss pocket knives. In terms of qualities, it is almost identical to X50CrMoV15 steel. It has excellent corrosion resistance, retains its sharpness for a long time, and is easy to sharpen.

52100 steel is a high-carbon, chromium-alloy steel (AISI 52100 bearing steel). Formerly a ball-bearing steel, only recently available in bar stock. Typical composition: 0.98-1.10% carbon, 1.30-1.60% chromium, 0.15-0.30% silicon, 0.25-0.45% manganese. The high carbon content provides excellent hardness and wear resistance, while chromium contributes notable strength, toughness, and resistance to corrosion. It is similar to 5160 but with around 1% carbon vs. 5160's ~0.60%, holds an edge better, but is less tough than 5160. Many consider it one of the finest kitchen knife steels available.

title: A2 Tool Steel
body: A2 Tool Steel is an air-hardening grade of steel that contains 5% chromium. A2 is noted for its good toughness and excellent dimensional stability in heat treatment. These characteristics make it a versatile tool steel that combines good performance and price. A2 falls between oil-hardening and D2 high-carbon, high chromium tool steels.

title: W2
body: Water hardening tool steel. Quite popular with custom knife makers, both beginners and seasoned experts. Easy to work with, decent edge holding, and ok toughness depending on the heat treatment. Maximum working hardness is in 63-65 HRC range. Carbon varies from 0.85-1.50%. W2 maxes out at 64-65 HRC when enough Carbon is present. Pretty good with a polished, thin edge at 64HRC. Found in various types of knives from small folders to large kitchen and utility knives. Overall decent steel, non-stainless, won't win awards in abrasive wear resistance, but will do a variety of jobs.

1095 is the most popular 10-series standard carbon steel (about 1% carbon) with low corrosion resistance and average edge retention properties. Edge Retention: 3/10. Corrosion Resistance: 2/10. Ease of Sharpening: 8/10. Why would you want 1095 steel? 1095 is a tough steel that's resistant to chipping, it's easy to sharpen, takes a crazy sharp edge, and is inexpensive to produce. The appeal is pure accessibility and sharpening ease.

title: Understanding Grinds
body: A 'Grind' refers to the shape and geometry of the blade's edge and down the blade. It determines how the knife cuts and interacts with food. Steel choice is NOT the most important variable when it comes to knife performance — Heat Treat and Blade Grind are generally the most fundamentally essential factors. Dr. Larrin Thomas (Knife Steel Nerds): 'While the choice of steel is important, grind and heat treatment are often considered more critical factors in determining a kitchen knife's performance, durability, and overall quality.' It doesn't matter how sharp your blade is; if it isn't ground well, it's not going to cut well. The edge makes the initial penetration but the blade's grind dictates how smoothly the rest of the blade's body follows along. Key definitions: Concave = curves inward (hollow grind). Convex = curves outward (convex grind). Spine = back of the blade opposite the edge. Primary Bevel/Grind = where the knife first begins to narrow into a cutting edge. Edge Bevel = the actual edge of the blade.

title: Hollow Grind
body: To make a hollow grind, the blade blank is applied to the surface of a grinding wheel, taking a concave scoop out of the blade. A full hollow grind goes from the edge all the way up to the spine. Hollow grinds remove a lot of material compared to other grinds, making a better slicer. As the blade does not increase in thickness as dramatically as other grinds, as you sharpen the edge it will remain nearly as thin as when you first got your knife — making hollow grinds typically easier to sharpen. However, since there is less material supporting the edge, it can chip or roll over with hard use. Strengths: Fantastic slicing ability, easy to sharpen, easier to manufacture. Best knife types: Skinners, hunting knives, small to medium EDC blades, straight razors. Weaknesses: The edge can be fragile, not suited for chopping.

title: Full Flat Grind
body: The full flat grind goes all the way down from the spine to the edge bevel in a flat, linear slope. The full flat grind is thickest at the spine for strength, but tapers down into a relatively thin edge for excellent slicing. The primary bevel slopes linearly and slowly, allowing the knife to pass through materials with more ease than other grinds. This is why the majority of kitchen knives are flat ground — so they can pass through food easily without much resistance. Strengths: Good cutting, strength, and chopping. Best Knife Types: EDC knives, kitchen knives, hunting knives — good on most knives. Weaknesses: Doesn't cut quite as well as a hollow grind, not quite as robust as a sabre grind.

title: Sabre Grind
body: A sabre grind (similar to a Japanese Wide Bevel) is either a flat or hollow grind where the primary bevel does not cover the entire width of the blade, leaving some portion unground. The transition line between the primary bevel and the unground portion is referred to as the Sabre Line. The sabre grind is used when the maker wants a stronger blade — often with thicker stock so the blade can stand up to hard use such as chopping. Classic military designs such as the Randall #1 and the Ka-bar Combat Knife utilize the sabre grind. Strengths: Excellent durability, will hold up to chopping or penetration. Best Knife Types: Military and Tactical knives, self-defense blades, camp knives. Weaknesses: Cutting ability is typically less impressive than other grind types.

title: Chisel Grind (Single Bevel)
body: The chisel grind is completely flat on one side, and has the primary bevel only on the other side. The chisel grind is easy to make as you only have to grind one side, and easy to sharpen for the same reason. The unaltered side can be sharpened at a thinner angle, making for a thin, sharp edge. However, achieving accurate cuts is difficult due to the unsymmetrical design — the blade will naturally slant towards the beveled side. This can be preferable with handmade Japanese sushi knives: when cutting fish quickly, a chisel grind allows the blade to cut away from your steadying hand. Strengths: Excellent strength, good chopping, easy to sharpen. Best Knife Types: Sometimes found in choppers and traditional handmade Japanese kitchen knives. Weaknesses: Cutting is not symmetrical; performance varies widely depending on grind angles.

title: Convex Grind
body: The convex grind arcs down into a convex curve towards the edge. Also known as the Moran Grind or Appleseed Grind, historically made with a hammer and now made with a slack belt grinder. Similar to the sabre grind in that it typically still has a lot of steel in the middle of the blade, making it the thickest of the three main types. This puts extra steel behind the edge, reinforcing and strengthening it. Technically the convex grind does not have an edge bevel — the grind curves all the way into the edge. The main drawback is that it can be difficult to sharpen; you need something flat with a little give (like a thick mouse pad with sandpaper) rather than traditional bench stones. Strengths: Very strong edge, great for chopping. Best Knife Types: Choppers, machetes, axes, some larger bushcraft knives. Weaknesses: Difficult to maintain and sharpen, requires uncommon sharpening tools.

title: Scandi Grind
body: The Scandinavian grind (Scandi grind) is a short flat or occasionally convex grind on a thin blade where the primary grind is also the edge bevel — meaning there is no secondary edge bevel/grind at all. Sometimes called a Zero Sabre Grind. This leaves a lot of material behind the edge, strengthening it. The benefit is that you can use the entire primary bevel to guide your knife along the bench stone as you sharpen it. The downside: you have to remove a lot of material when sharpening, since you have to sharpen the entire primary bevel. Do not turn a knife with an edge bevel into a scandi grind — if the maker designed it to have an edge bevel, this will often make the blade too thin with a weak edge. Strengths: Theory of sharpening is easy to understand, often has a strong edge. Weaknesses: Not as good at slicing, sharpening can be a chore.

title: German/French Chef's Knife vs Japanese Gyuto
body: (1) Blade Profile: French/German knives have a more curved blade profile with a deeper belly, facilitating the rocking motion common in Western cooking. Japanese gyutos often have a flatter blade profile, allowing for more efficient push-cut and pull-cut techniques. (2) Edge Geometry: French/German knives usually have a wider angle (approximately 20-25 degrees per side) for more durability but slightly less sharpness. Gyutos often have a narrower angle (approximately 15 degrees per side) for sharper cutting performance and precision. (3) Construction: French/German knives are traditionally made from softer stainless or carbon steel with more resilience. Gyutos are typically made from harder high-carbon steel for better edge retention. (4) Weight and Balance: French/German knives tend to be heavier with more weight towards the rear, assisting in chopping. Gyutos are generally lighter and more balanced for greater precision. Note: Many gyutos are not made exclusively for push/pull cuts — look for flat spots in the blade profile to determine cutting technique compatibility.

title: Nashiji (Pear Skin)
body: Nashiji (pear-skin) is a bi-product of forging. This finish is created by polishing away the black scale leftover from the forging process while leaving behind the resulting rough texture. It creates a super rustic look iconic to Japanese knives. Pros: Much like hammered finishes, Nashiji gives more grippiness and food release, but less noticeably. Perfect for those who want a little extra pizazz without being too in-your-face. Cons: More potential for moisture to settle into the textured finish, which can cause more potential for rusting when air drying knives, even on stainless steel.

title: Kurouchi (As Forged)
body: Kurouchi is forge scale — a coating of oxide that forms on iron heated to higher temperatures. It gives a pleasing black textured finish. Pros: Kurouchi wears and changes over time (wabi-sabi aesthetic). Can provide more grip when holding the blade than smoother finishes. May allow food to stick less to the blade. Can provide a moisture barrier that helps slow down and prevent rust on carbon steel knives. Cons: If you want a knife that always looks like new, this probably isn't for you. It can give more surface area for moisture to cling to, requiring you to dry the knife more carefully after use. Remember: it's stainLESS, not stainNEVER.

title: Tsuchime (Hammered)
body: Tsuchime means 'hammered.' This finish is created by hammering the knife repeatedly along the face to create an indented finish, giving each blade a unique texture. Some blacksmiths even custom-make their own hammers for funkier appearances. Pros: Can give more traction when pinch-gripping the blade. Great with food release because there are tons of little air pockets trapped between the blade and food — basically less suction! Cons: More potential for moisture to settle in those hammer marks, and you can sometimes rust the cladding steel by not wiping off your knife after use.

title: Migaki (Polished)
body: The Migaki (polished) finish is the most simple and commonly used. Minimalist in style, it is accomplished by buffing and polishing the blade until it's shiny and consistent but not quite fully mirrored. There is so much variety in how a Migaki finish can look, depending on how it's done. A machine-made Migaki can look very different from a smaller maker's laborious, clean and precise finish. Migaki finishes can range from more cloudy and matte all the way up to borderline mirror polished. Pros: No extra bells and whistles — just a clean, minimalist look. Excellent finish if you need minimal drag against the ingredients, like cutting sashimi and other delicate foods. Cons: Scratches can be more noticeable, and food tends to hang on tighter to this polished finish.

title: Suminagashi / Damascus
body: Most Damascus knives are clad in layered steel, conventionally referred to as damascus. It is often called suminagashi in Japan, as it resembles a traditional dying method of the same name. Suminagashi translates into 'floating ink' and references a paper and fabric dyeing technique dating back to the 12th century. While most are layered by the steel maker and not folded the traditional way, the core steel does the heavy lifting, and the damascus cladding is there to make the knife super pretty and more durable. Pros: Eye-catching and beautiful — jaw-dropping, especially as a gift. Shows the blacksmith's craft through unique hammer strike patterns. Various patterns available (mirrored, acid-etched, kurouchi, raindrops, frost, etc.). Cons: Damascus finishes require more work from the steel maker and the blacksmith — they usually come at a premium price.

title: Mirror Polish
body: Mirror Polished knives are the most labour-intensive finish to accomplish and the most difficult to maintain. Mirror polishing is done by progressively smoothing out imperfections from the surface of a blade by using multiple grits and buffing until the surface is smooth and shiny enough to achieve a mirrored surface. Pros: The best finish for knives designed for slicing tasks. Great for Sujihiki, Yanagiba, or a 240-270mm Gyuto. This slick finish creates less pull when slicing. Cons: You must be utterly gentle — no scratching motions from using, honing, wiping, or cleaning. Often these are display knives or for very special occasions only. Highly polished finishes also cause food (especially starchy vegetables) to stick more to the surface compared to rougher finishes.

title: What is Heat Treatment
body: Heat treatment is an essential part of the knife manufacturing process. It involves heating a metal or alloy to a specific temperature and then cooling it to harden the material, improving its ability to withstand wear and tear. Heat treatment can be used at different stages in the manufacturing process to change certain properties: making the metal stronger, harder, more durable, or more ductile depending on what the material needs. Notable industries where heat treatment plays an important role include aircraft, automobiles, hardware (saws and axes), computers, spacecraft, and military.

title: How Heat Treatment Works
body: The metal or alloy is heated up to a specified temperature (sometimes as hot as 2400 degrees F), held at that temperature for a certain amount of time (the 'soak time'), and then cooled. While it's hot, the metal's microstructure changes, resulting in changed physical properties. Metal soaked for a long amount of time will see different microstructure changes than metal soaked for a shorter period. The cooling process also plays a part — metal may be cooled quickly (quenching) or slowly in the furnace. The combination of the soak temperature, soak time, cooling temperature, and cooling duration all play a role.

title: Types of Heat Treatment
body: Common forms of heat treatment include: (1) Hardening: The metal is heated to a point where the elements transform into a solution, increasing the hardness and making it less malleable. (2) Annealing: Materials are heated to a certain temperature, held until transformation occurs, and then slowly air-dried. This softens the metal, making it more workable and less likely to fracture or crack. (3) Tempering: The metal is heated to a temperature lower than the critical point to reduce brittleness and maintain hardness. (4) Case Hardening: The outside of the material is hardened while the inside remains soft. (5) Normalization: Similar to annealing, makes the steel more tough and ductile by heating to critical temperatures until transformation occurs.

title: Why Heat Treatment Matters for Knives
body: Heat treatment involves heating and cooling the steel to optimize its hardness, toughness, and resilience. Proper heat treatment is crucial for achieving the desired balance of hardness and toughness, which directly impacts edge retention, sharpness, and durability. A well-treated blade can maintain its edge for longer periods and resist chipping or deformation during use. Even knives made from high-quality steel can underperform if not properly ground and heat-treated. Conversely, a well-crafted blade with an optimal grind and heat treatment can outperform knives made from superior steel but lacking proper craftsmanship. An expensive knife is not guaranteed to cut any better than a cheaper one — how that steel is processed plays a huge role in the knife's performance in the long run.

title: Japanese Knifemaking Regions Overview
body: Several knifemaking regions of Japan have signature elements or styles. The makers generally adhere to the style and methods of their area but it isn't strictly adhered to. While getting a knife from a particular 'company' might sound like the right way to go, it's oftentimes easier to decide what smith you would like to get and find the companies that he works with. You can further refine things if you are specific about which sharpener you want also — for example, Nakagawa and Y. Tanaka both run their own Hamono (knife making shop) and do produce knives under that name but they have worked with a variety of different sharpeners and many different brands. In non-Japanese makers, it's not uncommon for the smith to be the sharpener as well.

title: Sakai Region
body: Sakai knives have a reputation of being thin, having a lightweight design, and a thin spine with a nice distal taper. The fit and finish of Sakai knives tends to be better than other regions, and the knives tend to have light convex or flat grinds with cladding, often of the soft-iron variety. Additionally, most Sakai knives have their length measured from the edge of the machi/tang, which means a Sakai knife will often times be 10-15mm shorter than described or as measured by other regions.

title: Echizen / Takefu Village Region
body: Echizen knives have a reputation for more flashy finishes, with little to no distal taper and commonly hollow grinds. The finishes offered are often unique methods of hammering resulting in interesting patterns above the shinogi line. It is much more common for Echizen knives to be clad in stainless-steel, though soft iron can still be found. Following the finish aesthetic, handles are often less traditional or classic in style, going for blingy color or uniqueness instead.

title: Sanjo Region
body: Sanjo knives have a reputation for being more rustic, robust, and heavier. Additionally, these knives often feature an extreme distal taper, starting with the spine being very thick and finishing at the same width as a typical Sakai tip width. Many Sanjo knives are ground with a convexity to a much more dramatic degree than standard Sakai knives.

title: Tosa Region
body: Tosa knives have a reputation similar to Sanjo knives but focused much more on being price efficient with simple grinds. The distal taper will not be as pronounced and the fit and finish will be lower than the other major regions. Tosa makers tend to offer excellent value for money.

title: Sakai Blacksmiths
body: Notable Sakai blacksmiths: (1) Hiroshi Ashi (Ashi Hamono) — known for precise and high-quality knife crafting. (2) Hirotsugu Tosa — renowned sharpener and polisher, especially with Sakai Takayuki. (3) Itsuo Doi — master blacksmith known for meticulous craftsmanship; his Aogami 2 has few peers. (4) Kenichi Shiraki (Shiraki Hamono) — highly respected blacksmith. (5) Kenji Togashi — known for skill in forging high-quality honyaki blades; his brother Kenya does most of his sharpening. (6) Satoshi Nakagawa (Kikuchiyo / Nakagawa Hamono) — young hotshot competent in about any steel; astounding breadth of work. (7) Shinichiro Yamamoto (Sakai Takayuki). (8) Tatsuo Ikeda (Japanese Knife Imports). (9) Yoshikazu Ikeda — revered blacksmith known for superior knife-making skills. (10) Yoshikazu Tanaka (Tanaka Hamono) — known for traditional forging techniques; his heat treatment is absolutely fantastic and he uses an annealing kiln which contributes to its quality.

title: Echizen / Takefu Blacksmiths
body: Notable Echizen/Takefu blacksmiths: Hideo Kitaoka — third-generation master, known for single-bevel knives. Hideo Takamura (Takamura Hamono) — renowned for sharpness and durability. Hiroshi Kato (Kintaro) — highly respected, hand-forged knives combining traditional techniques with modern design. Isamu Takamura (Takamura Hamono) — contributing to the family reputation for excellence. Katsushige Anryu — fourth-generation blacksmith instrumental in shaping the Anryu brand. Katsuyasu Kamo — known for high-carbon steels and traditional forging. Makoto Kurosaki — innovative approach combining traditional techniques with modern materials. Masanobu Okada — high-quality knives both functional and aesthetically pleasing. Shiro Kamo — master blacksmith from Takefu Knife Village. Shungo Ogata — functional and artistic knives. Takeshi Saji — master blacksmith with handcrafted knives with unique designs and patterns. Takumi Ikeda — continuing the legacy of his mentor Katsushige Anryu. Terakazu Takamura — renowned for sharpness and edge retention. Yu Kurosaki — young blacksmith known for innovative and artistic knife designs. Yoshimi Kato (Kintaro) — son of Hiroshi Kato, continues the family tradition. Also: Kazuo Nomura, Kazuyoshi Honda, Masutani Kunio, Nao Yamamoto, Shigeki Tanaka, Yoshihiro Yauji.

title: Sanjo Blacksmiths
body: Notable Sanjo blacksmiths: Izuka-san (Shigefusa) — meticulous craftsmanship using traditional techniques, apprenticed under legendary Nagashima-san; forges all steel in-house including his own damascus called Kitaeji, uses Swedish carbon steel. Kazuomi Yamamoto (Yoshikane Hamono) — celebrated workshop with history dating back to 1919; known for SKD steel. Kouiti Turumaki (Munetoshi) — high-quality affordable knives with traditional craftsmanship. Masashi Yamamoto — known for Aogami Super steel knives. Mutsumi Hinoura — continues family tradition of knifemaking. Naoki Mazaki — highly regarded for craftsmanship; known for Aogami Super steel. Osamu Takeishi (Heiji) — robust knives with emphasis on functionality and durability. Shinichi Watanabe — custom-made knives with unique aesthetic and exceptional performance. Shuji Toyama — high-quality traditional Japanese knives, often with Aogami Super steel. Tsukasa Hinoura — master blacksmith with 30+ years of experience. Toshihiro Wakui — beautiful and functional knives combining Shirogami and Aogami steels.

title: Tosa Blacksmiths
body: Notable Tosa blacksmiths: Kosuke Muneishi — third-generation blacksmith from Tosa, known for Aogami (blue steel) knives with kurouchi finish; family business started in 1955. Kyohei Shindo — meticulous craftsmanship with sharp edges and ease of handling. Makoto Tadokoro — from Echizen, exceptional sharpness and balance. Michikuni Tokaji — respected within Japan for sharpness and durability. Suzuki-san (Tosaichi Hamono) — well-regarded firm producing a wide range of traditional Japanese knives. Tsutomu Kajiwara — master blacksmith from Tosa, known for blue steel core with soft iron cladding. Tsunehisa — brand representing a collective of skilled artisans, popular among both professional chefs and enthusiasts.

title: Japanese Knife Sharpeners
body: Prominent Japanese knife sharpeners who work with various smiths and brands: Ashi Hamono (Gesshin Ginga), Kei Kobayashi (Kobayashi Knives), Makoto Kurosaki, Mitsuaki Takada (Yohei / Takada no Hamono), Morihiro (Kambei), Myojin Naohito, Yauchi Tsuyoshi (Kyuzo). Note that the sharpener can have a significant effect on the cutting performance of a knife — for example, Nakagawa blades sharpened by Kyuzo, Morihiro, Myojin, or Nishida can have noticeably different cutting characteristics.
